transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um, I hope I'm explaining this right, but... I guess what finally made me make an appointment is just some minor stuff at work? I'm an advertising sales agent, and we have these really long strategy meetings. 

I know I’m supposed to just stay seated and listen, but I just... I keep getting up. I'll find little excuses, like going to refill my water bottle, or I'll just sort of pace over by the printer for a minute. It's really not a huge deal, I still get my work done, but I worry it might look a little unprofessional to my boss? I don't know, is that the kind of thing I should be bringing up here?

How long have you been experiencing this difficulty staying seated and needing to move around? Has this always been something you've struggled with, or is it something newer that's been bothering you?

Well, um... I guess it really started to stand out to me about two years and two months ago? That's when I switched into this advertising sales strategy role. Before that, my jobs were a bit more active, so I don't think it was as obvious. Or, you know, maybe I just managed it better then? I really hope I'm not making a bigger deal out of this than it is. Does that timeline make sense for what you're asking?

When you're sitting in those meetings and feel the urge to get up and move around, does it feel like there's a physical restlessness or tension in your body that makes it hard to stay still, or does it feel more like anxiety or worry about the situation?

Um, I wouldn't really say it's anxiety or worry. I like my job and the people I work with, so I'm not nervous about being there. It's more just... I don't know, a little bit of physical restlessness, I guess? 

Like, it's not a huge deal, it's just this slight feeling like I have extra energy that I need to burn off, so my legs just want to stretch. It's not like I'm jumping out of my skin or anything crazy like that. It's very manageable, really. Does that sound like what you meant by physical restlessness, or am I explaining it wrong?

When you were a child or teenager, did you ever have similar difficulties with sitting still or feelings of restlessness, or is this something that's really only started happening since you changed jobs two years ago?

Um, well... I guess if I really think back, it's probably been there for a while? I mean, I don't want to sound like I was a bad kid or anything, because I really wasn't! But, um, I do remember my teachers back in elementary school—so way before high school—saying some things on my report cards. 

They always said I was bright, which was nice! But they also mentioned I tended to rush through my work, or, you know, I'd talk out of turn sometimes. And I guess I forgot my homework a bit, and my desk was always full of half-finished papers. But I think a lot of kids are like that, right? Just a little disorganized and eager to participate? I hope that doesn't make me sound like I was a problem student... is that the kind of childhood stuff you were looking for?
When you're working on tasks or projects, do you find it hard to concentrate and stay focused on one thing, or do you tend to get distracted easily?

Oh, um... well, I really try my best to stay on top of things, because I want to do a good job for my team. But, I guess sometimes... like, if we're in one of those longer strategy meetings, or if I'm reading through a really dense client brief? 

I always start out super focused and ready to go. But then, after a few minutes, I'll just suddenly realize that I've been staring at the exact same slide, or the same paragraph, and I have absolutely no idea what the last point even was. 

I always catch myself and try to reread it right away, though! I'm sure everyone gets a little spacey during long meetings or when there's a lot of text, right? I really hope that doesn't make me sound like I'm not dedicated to my work or that I'm just zoning out on purpose. Does that sound like the kind of distraction you were asking about?

Besides talking out of turn in class that you mentioned, do you find yourself interrupting people or blurting things out in conversations at work or in other situations, or is that more of a thing from your childhood?

Um, I guess it does still happen sometimes, yeah. But I really don't mean to be rude or anything! I just... I get really excited about the work, and I want to be helpful, you know? 

So sometimes, if a client or a coworker is asking a question, I think I know exactly what they're going to ask, and I just... kind of jump in with the answer before they're actually finished talking. And then, unfortunately, I'll realize that I totally misunderstood where they were going with it, or I just ended up cutting them off. 

I always apologize right away, of course! I really try to be respectful of everyone's time and input. I just get a little too eager to help, I think. Is that... is that normal for people who are just really enthusiastic about their jobs, or is that a bad thing to admit?

Looking back at your school years, did these issues with focusing, rushing through work, or talking out of turn ever cause problems for you—like getting in trouble with teachers, affecting your grades, or making it harder to do well academically?

Um, well... back in school, I wouldn't say it caused *huge* problems. I mean, my grades were mostly fine! I got my degree and everything. The teachers would just put those little notes on my report cards, but I was never, like, sent to the principal's office or anything bad like that. I really tried to be a good student.

But, um... I guess lately, it has been causing a little bit of trouble. Just... just at work. I really don't want you to think I'm bad at my job, because I do care so much about doing good work and making sure my clients are happy! But... um... 

It's just that recently, some of these things have started showing up in my performance reviews. My manager mentioned that I need to be more detail-oriented. And... well, there was this one time a client actually complained. I had rushed through some of their materials and missed some important details, and they felt like they couldn't trust me with the account. 

That really, really upset me, because the last thing I want to do is damage an account or make someone feel like I don't care. I always try to fix my mistakes immediately! But that one complaint really made me worry. Is it... I mean, do a lot of people have little hiccups like that at work when they're managing a lot of accounts? I really hope it doesn't sound like I'm failing at my job...

When you think back to elementary school, around ages 6 to 12, would you say these kinds of things—like the restlessness, difficulty focusing, rushing through work, and talking out of turn—were happening pretty regularly back then, or did they really only become noticeable after you started your current job?

Oh, um... no, it definitely wasn't just at this job. I remember it starting way, way before high school. Like, back in elementary school, for sure. 

My teachers were always really sweet, though, and they always made sure to write that I was bright! I really liked school and wanted to do well. But... they did also write that I rushed through my work a lot. And, yeah, the talking out of turn was definitely happening back then, too. 

I also... well, I'd forget my homework sometimes. And if you looked inside my desk, it was... um, kind of embarrassing, honestly. It was just stuffed with all these half-finished papers. But I really wasn't trying to be messy or a bad student! I think I just got so excited about new activities that I'd forget to finish the old ones or put them away properly. 

A lot of kids have messy desks and forget things at that age, though, right? I really hope that doesn't make me sound like I was a problem child or totally out of control... I was always trying my best to be good!

When you got to middle school and high school, did these same kinds of things—the restlessness, difficulty focusing, and interrupting people—continue to happen, or did they get better as you got older?

Um, I think... I think things actually got a bit better in middle and high school? Or, well, maybe I just figured out how to manage it better because I really, really wanted to get into a good college and make my teachers proud. I was always trying so hard to be a good student, so I wouldn't say it was a huge problem back then. 

But, um... honestly, it's really just been noticeably affecting me much more recently. Specifically, since I changed into advertising sales strategy... which was about two years and two months ago. It's a wonderful role, and I'm so grateful they trusted me with it! But there's just a lot more independent work to juggle, and I think that's when these little hiccups really started getting in the way of things. 

Is that... does that happen to a lot of people when they take on a more strategic role? I just really hope it doesn't seem like I can't handle my job, because I really do love it and want to do well!

When you were in middle school and high school, even though you say things got better, were you still experiencing that physical restlessness—like needing to move around or stretch your legs—during classes or while studying, or did that pretty much go away during those years?

Um, well, in middle school and high school... I think the physical restlessness wasn't too bad. I mean, I was involved in a lot of after-school activities, so I had plenty of chances to move around! I really tried hard to sit still during class because I didn't want to disrupt the teachers or the other students. 

But, um... actually, part of the reason I finally decided to come in and talk to you is because of something happening now. It's just... I've been having a really hard time staying in my seat during these long sales strategy meetings at work. I know I'm supposed to just sit there and listen, and I really want to be respectful of whoever is presenting! But I just find myself making up little excuses to get up. Like, I'll go refill my water bottle, or I'll just sort of pace over by the printer for a second. 

I try to be really quiet and not bother anyone when I do it! But I know it's probably not the most professional thing to do when everyone else is sitting perfectly still. Do you think... I mean, is it normal to just need to stretch your legs during really long meetings? I just don't want my team to think I'm not paying attention or that I don't care about the strategy, because I really, really do!

You mentioned that your manager gave you feedback about being more detail-oriented, and there was a client complaint about missed details. Besides those work issues, have these kinds of problems—like rushing through things, missing details, or having trouble focusing—caused you significant difficulties in other areas of your life, like in your relationships, managing your finances, or other important responsibilities?

Um, well... I really try hard not to let it affect my personal life. I mean, my friends and family know I can be a little scatterbrained sometimes, but I always try to make up for it by being really supportive and present when we're together! And I'm usually pretty okay with paying my bills on time, mostly because I set up a lot of automatic payments so I don't have to worry about forgetting. 

But, um... honestly, it's really just the work stuff that's been weighing on me the most. Like you mentioned, my manager brought up the detail-oriented thing in my performance review. And... well, that one client complaint was really, really hard for me to hear. I just felt awful about it. It made me so worried that I might actually damage our accounts or lose client trust, even though I care so, so much about doing good work for them! 

I just... I want my manager and the clients to know that I'm really dedicated and trying my best. It's just so frustrating when these little mistakes slip through. Does that make sense? I really hope it doesn't sound like I'm careless, because I promise I'm not trying to be!

You mentioned that things got better in middle and high school, but then these issues started showing up again more noticeably about two years ago when you changed jobs. Between high school and two years ago—so during college and your earlier jobs—would you say you weren't really experiencing these kinds of problems at all, or were they still there but just not causing you as much trouble?

Um, I'd say... I mean, in college and my first few jobs, I really didn't notice them much at all? I was always so focused on doing everything right and making sure my professors and bosses were happy with my work. I mean, maybe I had moments where I was a little disorganized or had to pull an all-nighter to finish a paper, but I always got it done! 

I really tried to be the person everyone could rely on, so I made sure to double-check everything back then. I don't think it was really an issue... at least, nobody ever complained about my work or told me I was missing things. I hope that's okay? Like, is it normal for these things to kind of go away for a while and then come back when you get a job that requires a lot more independent strategy? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline for all this!

But there's just a lot more independent work to juggle, and I think that's when these little hiccups really started getting in the way of things. 

Is that... does that happen to a lot of people when they take on a more strategic role? I just really hope it doesn't seem like I can't handle my job, because I really do love it and want to do well!

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient meets duration criteria for ADHD by clarifying if symptoms were present persistently throughout childhood and adolescence, or if they genuinely improved/resolved during those years and only re-emerged recently.
doctor.question: When you were in middle school and high school, even though you say things got better, were you still experiencing that physical restlessness—like needing to move around or stretch your legs—during classes or while studying, or did that pretty much go away during those years?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: Honestly, what made me come in is that I keep getting up during long sales strategy meetings when I know I’m supposed to stay seated, even if it’s just to refill water or pace by the printer.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical restlessness and needing to move around or stretch legs during classes, which maps to the symptom of leaving one's seat when expected to remain seated.

patient.answer:
Um, well, in middle school and high school... I think the physical restlessness wasn't too bad. I mean, I was involved in a lot of after-school activities, so I had plenty of chances to move around! I really tried hard to sit still during class because I didn't want to disrupt the teachers or the other students. 

But, um... actually, part of the reason I finally decided to come in and talk to you is because of something happening now. It's just... I've been having a really hard time staying in my seat during these long sales strategy meetings at work. I know I'm supposed to just sit there and listen, and I really want to be respectful of whoever is presenting! But I just find myself making up little excuses to get up. Like, I'll go refill my water bottle, or I'll just sort of pace over by the printer for a second. 

I try to be really quiet and not bother anyone when I do it! But I know it's probably not the most professional thing to do when everyone else is sitting perfectly still. Do you think... I mean, is it normal to just need to stretch your legs during really long meetings? I just don't want my team to think I'm not paying attention or that I don't care about the strategy, because I really, really do!

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's symptoms have caused clinically significant impairment in multiple life domains (work, social, academic) or just minor functional difficulties, which is crucial for distinguishing ADHD from normal variation
doctor.question: You mentioned that your manager gave you feedback about being more detail-oriented, and there was a client complaint about missed details. Besides those work issues, have these kinds of problems—like rushing through things, missing details, or having trouble focusing—caused you significant difficulties in other areas of your life, like in your relationships, managing your finances, or other important responsibilities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, it has started showing up in performance reviews and client trust; one client complaint especially made me worry that I could damage accounts even though I care a lot about doing good work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the symptoms on various areas of my life, which directly addresses the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Um, well... I really try hard not to let it affect my personal life. I mean, my friends and family know I can be a little scatterbrained sometimes, but I always try to make up for it by being really supportive and present when we're together! And I'm usually pretty okay with paying my bills on time, mostly because I set up a lot of automatic payments so I don't have to worry about forgetting. 

But, um... honestly, it's really just the work stuff that's been weighing on me the most. Like you mentioned, my manager brought up the detail-oriented thing in my performance review. And... well, that one client complaint was really, really hard for me to hear. I just felt awful about it. It made me so worried that I might actually damage our accounts or lose client trust, even though I care so, so much about doing good work for them! 

I just... I want my manager and the clients to know that I'm really dedicated and trying my best. It's just so frustrating when these little mistakes slip through. Does that make sense? I really hope it doesn't sound like I'm careless, because I promise I'm not trying to be!

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient meets the duration criterion for ADHD (symptoms present for at least 6 months) by clarifying the timeline of symptom onset and establishing whether symptoms have been continuously present since childhood or if there were periods of remission.
doctor.question: You mentioned that things got better in middle and high school, but then these issues started showing up again more noticeably about two years ago when you changed jobs. Between high school and two years ago—so during college and your earlier jobs—would you say you weren't really experiencing these kinds of problems at all, or were they still there but just not causing you as much trouble?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's experience during college and earlier jobs, which is not specifically covered by any item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um, I'd say... I mean, in college and my first few jobs, I really didn't notice them much at all? I was always so focused on doing everything right and making sure my professors and bosses were happy with my work. I mean, maybe I had moments where I was a little disorganized or had to pull an all-nighter to finish a paper, but I always got it done! 

I really tried to be the person everyone could rely on, so I made sure to double-check everything back then. I don't think it was really an issue... at least, nobody ever complained about my work or told me I was missing things. I hope that's okay? Like, is it normal for these things to kind of go away for a while and then come back when you get a job that requires a lot more independent strategy? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline for all this!

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to the clinic today
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a longstanding history of ADHD symptoms dating back to elementary school (ages 6-12), including restlessness, difficulty sustaining attention, rushing through work, talking out of turn, and organizational difficulties. While symptoms were partially compensated for during high school and college through increased effort and structure, they have re-emerged and are now causing functional impairment in the workplace (performance review feedback about detail-orientation, client complaint regarding missed details). The pattern is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Combined Presentation, with symptoms present since childhood and current functional impairment in occupational domain.
